title: Der starke Hans
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 166. Text from Wikisource („Der starke Hans (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly. The 1857 edition prints this tale with a single paragraph break, which is preserved here; the further paragraphing is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: A boy carried off as a small child by robbers and raised in their cave grows up with the strength of a giant, and uses it to win his mother's freedom and then his own way in the world, fighting robbers and monsters as he goes. It is one of Grimm's rowdier adventure tales, closer to a folk epic of feats than to a fireside story, and it does not look away from the violence of the escape.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Mann und eine Frau, die hatten nur ein einziges Kind, und lebten in einem abseits gelegenen Thale ganz allein.
sentences.l: There was once a man and a woman, they had only one single child, and lived in a valley lying off to one side quite alone.
sentences.i: There was once a man and a woman who had but one single child, and lived quite alone in an out-of-the-way valley.
sentences.n: The 1857 printing breaks this tale only once, and that break is kept exactly where it stands; the further paragraphing here has been supplied so the tale can be read on a screen, and not a word of the German is altered. “die hatten” is a demonstrative, not a relative — the German begins afresh, they had, the way a story told aloud does. Thal is the 1857 spelling of Tal, valley; the th- of Thal, Thür and Thier is one of this book’s constant marks.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß die Mutter einmal ins Holz gieng, Tannenreiser zu lesen, und den kleinen Hans, der erst zwei Jahr alt war, mitnahm.
sentences.l: It bore itself to, that the mother once went into the wood to gather fir-twigs, and took little Hans, who was only two years old, along.
sentences.i: It came to pass that the mother went one day into the wood to gather fir-twigs, and took little Hans, who was only two years old, along with her.
sentences.n: “es trägt sich zu” is it comes to pass; zutragen is separable and its particle zu stands at the end. lesen here has its old sense, to gather, to pick up — the one still alive in Ähren lesen, to glean. mitnehmen splits too, and mit closes the clause. “zwei Jahr” keeps the singular after a number, as older German does.

sentences.t: Da es gerade in der Frühlingszeit war und das Kind seine Freude an den bunten Blumen hatte, so gieng sie immer weiter mit ihm in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: Since it was just in the spring-time and the child had its delight in the brightly coloured flowers, she went ever further with him into the wood in.
sentences.i: As it was just the spring of the year, and the child took delight in the bright flowers, she went further and further with him into the wood.
sentences.n: da at the head of a clause with its verb at the end means since, because. “seine Freude an etwas haben” is to take delight in a thing. hineingehen splits its particle in two halves that stand at opposite ends of the phrase — “in den Wald hinein” — which is how German gets both direction and destination into one sentence.

sentences.t: Plötzlich sprangen aus dem Gebüsch zwei Räuber hervor, packten die Mutter und das Kind und führten sie tief in den schwarzen Wald, wo Jahr aus Jahr ein kein Mensch hinkam.
sentences.l: Suddenly there sprang out of the bushes two robbers forth, seized the mother and the child and led them deep into the black wood, where year out year in no person came.
sentences.i: Suddenly two robbers sprang out of the bushes, seized the mother and the child, and led them deep into the black wood, where from one year’s end to the next no one ever came.
sentences.n: hervorspringen splits, and hervor closes its clause long after the subject has arrived. “Jahr aus Jahr ein” is the fixed phrase, with the halves in the reverse of the English year in, year out. hinkommen is to get to a place.

sentences.t: Die arme Frau bat die Räuber inständig sie mit ihrem Kinde frei zu lassen, aber das Herz der Räuber war von Stein: sie hörten nicht auf ihr Bitten und Flehen und trieben sie mit Gewalt an weiter zu gehen.
sentences.l: The poor woman begged the robbers urgently to let her go free with her child, but the heart of the robbers was of stone: they did not listen to her begging and pleading and drove her on with force to go further.
sentences.i: The poor woman begged the robbers urgently to let her and her child go free, but the robbers’ hearts were of stone: they would not listen to her begging and pleading, and drove her on by force to walk further.
sentences.n: Bitten and Flehen are ordinary verbs turned into nouns simply by capitalising them — German makes nouns of infinitives freely, and this book does it constantly. antreiben is separable and its an sits at the end, so the sentence reads “trieben sie … an”. inständig is urgently, insistently.

sentences.t: Nachdem sie etwa zwei Stunden durch Stauden und Dörner sich hatten durcharbeiten müssen, kamen sie zu einem Felsen, wo eine Thüre war, an welche die Räuber klopften, und die sich alsbald öffnete.
sentences.l: After they had had to work their way through shrubs and thorns for about two hours, they came to a rock, where there was a door, at which the robbers knocked, and which opened at once.
sentences.i: After they had had to work their way for some two hours through scrub and thorns, they came to a rock where there was a door; the robbers knocked at it, and it opened at once.
sentences.n: When a modal verb stands in a perfect tense, German puts the modal itself into the infinitive at the very end — “hatten … müssen” and not gemußt. Dörner is the older plural of Dorn, modern Dornen. Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Tür.

sentences.t: Sie mußten durch einen langen dunkelen Gang und kamen endlich in eine große Höhle, die von einem Feuer, das auf dem Herd brannte, erleuchtet war.
sentences.l: They had to through a long dark passage and came at last into a great cave, which was lit by a fire that burned on the hearth.
sentences.i: They had to pass down a long dark passage, and came at last into a great cave lit by a fire that burned on the hearth.
sentences.n: “sie mußten durch einen Gang” has no verb of motion in it at all: with a modal and a direction, German can leave the going unsaid, and the literal line above keeps that gap open. dunkelen is an older inflected form of dunkel. A cave with a hearth in it — the robbers are keeping house here, which is why they will want a housekeeper.

sentences.t: An der Wand hiengen Schwerter, Säbel und andere Mordgewehre, die in dem Lichte blinkten, und in der Mitte stand ein schwarzer Tisch, an dem vier andere Räuber saßen und spielten, und oben an saß der Hauptmann.
sentences.l: On the wall hung swords, sabres and other murder-weapons, which glinted in the light, and in the middle stood a black table, at which four other robbers sat and played, and at the top end sat the captain.
sentences.i: On the wall hung swords, sabres and other murderous weapons that glinted in the light; in the middle stood a black table, at which four other robbers sat playing, and at the head of it sat the captain.
sentences.n: Mordgewehr is Mord, murder, with Gewehr, which in older German is any weapon and not only a gun. “oben an” marks the head of the table, the place of honour. hiengen is the 1857 spelling of hingen.

sentences.t: Dieser kam, als er die Frau sah, herbei, redete sie an und sagte sie sollte nur ruhig und ohne Angst sein, sie thäten ihr nichts zu Leid,
sentences.l: This one came, when he saw the woman, over, addressed her and said she should only be calm and without fear, they would do her nothing to harm,
sentences.i: When he saw the woman he came over, spoke to her, and said that she should only be calm and have no fear — they would do her no harm;
sentences.n: Two separable verbs in a row hold their particles back to the end of their clauses: “kam … herbei” and “redete sie an”. From “sie sollte” onward the German shifts into the subjunctive of reported speech — sollte, thäten, müßte, hielte — so his terms are given in his own voice with no quotation marks at all. “jemandem etwas zu Leid thun” is to do a person harm.

sentences.t: aber sie müßte das Hauswesen besorgen, und wenn sie alles in Ordnung hielte, so sollte sie es nicht schlimm bei ihnen haben.
sentences.l: but she would have to see to the housekeeping, and if she kept everything in order, then she should not have it bad with them.
sentences.i: but she would have to see to the housekeeping, and if she kept everything in order she should not fare badly with them.
sentences.n: “es gut oder schlimm haben” is to fare well or badly. müßte and hielte carry on the reported speech begun in the sentence before. Das Hauswesen is the whole running of a household.

sentences.t: Darauf gaben sie ihr etwas zu essen und zeigten ihr ein Bett, wo sie mit ihrem Kinde schlafen könnte.
sentences.l: Thereupon they gave her something to eat and showed her a bed where she could sleep with her child.
sentences.n: könnte is subjunctive because the bed is being offered rather than described — a bed where she might sleep. Darauf is thereupon, the plain way this book steps from one action to the next. Nothing is said of how the woman took the offer, and the tale is about to leap years forward in a single sentence.

sentences.t: Die Frau blieb viele Jahre bei den Räubern, und Hans ward groß und stark.
sentences.l: The woman stayed many years with the robbers, and Hans became big and strong.
sentences.n: This is the sentence at which the 1857 printing begins a new paragraph, and it is the only such break in the whole tale. ward is the old form of wurde and carries much of the past tense in this book.

sentences.t: Die Mutter erzählte ihm Geschichten und lehrte ihn in einem alten Ritterbuch, das sie in der Höhle fand, lesen.
sentences.l: The mother told him stories and taught him in an old book of knights, that she found in the cave, to read.
sentences.i: The mother told him stories and taught him to read out of an old book of knights’ tales that she had found in the cave.
sentences.n: The infinitive lesen waits past the whole relative clause to the very end of the sentence — German holds its verbs back, and the reader learns only at the close what she was teaching him. A Ritterbuch is a chapbook of knightly romances, the common reading of the time. lehren takes two accusatives: taught him the thing.

sentences.t: Als Hans neun Jahr alt war, machte er sich aus einem Tannenast einen starken Knüttel und versteckte ihn hinter das Bett:
sentences.l: When Hans was nine years old, he made himself out of a fir-branch a strong cudgel and hid it behind the bed:
sentences.i: When Hans was nine years old he made himself a stout cudgel out of a fir branch, and hid it behind the bed;
sentences.n: “machte er sich” is the dative of advantage — made for himself. “hinter das Bett” takes the accusative because it answers where to, not where. The cudgel appears here and does all the work of the first half of the tale.

sentences.t: dann gieng er zu seiner Mutter und sprach „liebe Mutter, sage mir jetzt einmal wer mein Vater ist, ich will und muß es wissen.“
sentences.l: then he went to his mother and spoke “dear mother, tell me now for once who my father is, I will and must know it.”
sentences.i: then he went to his mother and said: “Dear mother, tell me now who my father is — I will and must know it.”
sentences.n: einmal after an imperative is not once but a nudge: go on, tell me. “ich will und muß es wissen” lets two modal verbs share a single infinitive at the end. sage is the imperative. He is nine years old and demanding this of a woman who has kept it from him deliberately.

sentences.t: Die Mutter schwieg still und wollte es ihm nicht sagen, damit er nicht das Heimweh bekäme: sie wußte auch daß die gottlosen Räuber den Hans doch nicht fortlassen würden;
sentences.l: The mother kept silent and would not tell it to him, so that he would not get the homesickness: she knew too that the godless robbers would not let Hans go after all;
sentences.i: The mother kept silent and would not tell him, so that he should not be seized with homesickness; she knew too that the godless robbers would never let Hans go;
sentences.n: “still schweigen” doubles the silence, since schweigen already means to be silent. bekäme is subjunctive after damit, marking a purpose rather than a fact. Heimweh is home-ache: the longing for a home Hans has never seen.

sentences.t: aber es hätte ihr fast das Herz zersprengt, daß Hans nicht sollte zu seinem Vater kommen.
sentences.l: but it would almost have burst her the heart, that Hans should not come to his father.
sentences.i: but it almost burst her heart that Hans should not come to his father.
sentences.n: “es hätte ihr … zersprengt” is the dative of possession again — burst the heart to her, where English says her heart. zersprengen is to burst a thing apart; the zer- prefix always carries that sense of breaking asunder.

sentences.t: In der Nacht, als die Räuber von ihrem Raubzug heimkehrten, holte Hans seinen Knüttel hervor, stellte sich vor den Hauptmann und sagte „jetzt will ich wissen wer mein Vater ist, und wenn du mirs nicht gleich sagst, so schlag ich dich nieder.“
sentences.l: In the night, when the robbers turned home from their robbing-raid, Hans fetched his cudgel forth, placed himself before the captain and said “now I will know who my father is, and if you do not tell me it at once, then I strike you down.”
sentences.i: In the night, when the robbers came home from their raid, Hans fetched out his cudgel, planted himself before the captain and said: “Now I mean to know who my father is, and if you do not tell me at once, I will strike you down.”
sentences.n: Three separable verbs stand in a row — hervorholen, heimkehren, niederschlagen — and each leaves its particle at the end of its own clause. mirs is mir and es run together, it to me. The boy is nine, and he addresses the captain of a robber band with du, as he would address anyone.

sentences.t: Da lachte der Hauptmann und gab dem Hans eine Ohrfeige, daß er unter den Tisch kugelte.
sentences.l: Then the captain laughed and gave Hans a box on the ear, so that he rolled under the table.
sentences.i: At that the captain laughed and gave Hans such a box on the ear that he went rolling under the table.
sentences.n: “dem Hans” — this book puts the definite article in front of a personal name freely, as spoken German still does in the south. kugeln is to roll like a ball, from die Kugel. daß here carries the force of so that, with the so left unsaid.

sentences.t: Hans machte sich wieder auf, schwieg und dachte „ich will noch ein Jahr warten und es dann noch einmal versuchen, vielleicht gehts besser.“
sentences.l: Hans got himself up again, kept silent and thought “I will wait one more year and then try it once again, perhaps it goes better.”
sentences.i: Hans picked himself up again, said nothing, and thought: “I will wait one more year and then try again — perhaps it will go better.”
sentences.n: “sich aufmachen” is to get oneself up and going, to set out. gehts is geht es with the pronoun swallowed into the verb. His thoughts are printed inside quotation marks exactly like speech, which this book does throughout.

sentences.t: Als das Jahr herum war, holte er seinen Knüttel wieder hervor, wischte den Staub ab, betrachtete ihn und sprach „es ist ein tüchtiger wackerer Knüttel.“
sentences.l: When the year was round, he fetched his cudgel out again, wiped the dust off, looked it over and spoke “it is a sturdy, sound cudgel.”
sentences.i: When the year had come round he fetched out his cudgel again, wiped off the dust, looked it over, and said: “It is a sturdy, serviceable cudgel.”
sentences.n: “herum sein” said of time is to be up, to have come round. wacker here is the High German word — sound, stout, serviceable — said of a thing that will not fail you, and not the Low German wacker, handsome. abwischen and hervorholen both leave their particles at the end.

sentences.t: Nachts kamen die Räuber heim, tranken Wein, einen Krug nach dem anderen, und fiengen an die Köpfe zu hängen.
sentences.l: At night the robbers came home, drank wine, one jug after the other, and began to hang their heads.
sentences.i: At night the robbers came home, drank wine, one jug after another, and began to let their heads droop.
sentences.n: “die Köpfe hängen” is said of men growing heavy and drowsy: heads sinking over the table. Nachts is an adverb formed out of a genitive, by night. anfangen splits, and “fiengen … an” frames the clause; fiengen is the 1857 spelling of fingen.

sentences.t: Da holte der Hans seinen Knüttel herbei, stellte sich wieder vor den Hauptmann und fragte ihn wer sein Vater wäre.
sentences.l: Then Hans fetched his cudgel over, placed himself again before the captain and asked him who his father was.
sentences.n: wäre is the subjunctive of reported speech: the question is given at second hand this time, not in his own words. The whole scene of a year before is repeated almost sentence for sentence, which is how these tales mark a second attempt.

sentences.t: Der Hauptmann gab ihm abermals eine so kräftige Ohrfeige, daß Hans unter den Tisch rollte,
sentences.l: The captain gave him once again so strong a box on the ear that Hans rolled under the table,
sentences.i: The captain gave him once again such a hearty box on the ear that Hans went rolling under the table,
sentences.n: abermals is once again, anew — an elevated word this book keeps for repeated actions. “so … daß” frames a consequence, exactly as English frames one with so … that.

sentences.t: aber es dauerte nicht lange, so war er wieder oben und schlug mit seinem Knüttel auf den Hauptmann und die Räuber, daß sie Arme und Beine nicht mehr regen konnten.
sentences.l: but it did not last long, then he was up again and struck with his cudgel on the captain and the robbers, so that they could stir arms and legs no more.
sentences.i: but it was not long before he was up again, and laid about the captain and the robbers with his cudgel until they could stir neither arm nor leg.
sentences.n: “es dauerte nicht lange, so …” is the ordinary German for it was not long before. “schlagen auf” with the accusative is to lay into somebody. regen is to stir, to move a limb. Nothing here is softened: a boy of ten beats six armed men into the floor, and the tale reports it as an achievement.

sentences.t: Die Mutter stand in einer Ecke und war voll Verwunderung über seine Tapferkeit und Stärke.
sentences.l: The mother stood in a corner and was full of astonishment over his bravery and strength.
sentences.i: The mother stood in a corner, full of astonishment at his bravery and strength.
sentences.n: “voll Verwunderung” takes no article, as such phrases of state do not in German. über after a word of feeling is at, about.

sentences.t: Als Hans mit seiner Arbeit fertig war, gieng er zu seiner Mutter und sagte „jetzt ist mirs Ernst gewesen, aber jetzt muß ich auch wissen wer mein Vater ist.“
sentences.l: When Hans was finished with his work, he went to his mother and said “now it has been earnest to me, but now I must also know who my father is.”
sentences.i: When Hans had finished his work he went to his mother and said: “This time I was in earnest — and now I must know who my father is.”
sentences.n: “es ist mir Ernst” is I am in earnest, with the person in the dative and Ernst standing as a noun. seine Arbeit — the beating is called his work, plainly and without any comment. mirs is mir and es run together again.

sentences.t: „Lieber Hans,“ antwortete die Mutter, „komm wir wollen gehen und ihn suchen bis wir ihn finden.“
sentences.l: “Dear Hans,” answered the mother, “come we will go and seek him until we find him.”
sentences.i: “Dear Hans,” answered the mother, “come — we will go and look for him until we find him.”
sentences.n: wollen here is not want but the plain first person plural of intention: we will, let us. The 1857 text prints komm with no comma after it, running the imperative straight into what follows.

sentences.t: Sie nahm dem Hauptmann den Schlüssel zu der Eingangsthüre ab, und Hans holte einen großen Mehlsack, packte Gold, Silber und was er sonst noch für schöne Sachen fand, zusammen, bis er voll war, und nahm ihn dann auf den Rücken.
sentences.l: She took the key to the entrance-door off the captain, and Hans fetched a great flour-sack, packed gold, silver and what other fine things he found together, until it was full, and then took it onto his back.
sentences.i: She took the key of the entrance door from the captain, and Hans fetched a great flour sack, packed into it gold, silver and whatever other fine things he found, until it was full, and then took it up on his back.
sentences.n: “jemandem etwas abnehmen” is to take a thing off somebody, with the person in the dative: “nahm dem Hauptmann … ab”. zusammenpacken splits too, and its zusammen has to wait through the whole list before it arrives. Nothing is said of what became of the beaten robbers; the tale simply walks past them.

sentences.t: Sie verließen die Höhle, aber was that Hans die Augen auf, als er aus der Finsternis heraus in das Tageslicht kam, und den grünen Wald, Blumen und Vögel und die Morgensonne am Himmel erblickte.
sentences.l: They left the cave, but how Hans opened his eyes up, when he came out of the darkness into the daylight, and caught sight of the green wood, flowers and birds and the morning sun in the sky.
sentences.i: They left the cave — and how Hans opened his eyes when he came out of the darkness into the daylight and caught sight of the green wood, the flowers and birds, and the morning sun in the sky.
sentences.n: “was that Hans die Augen auf” uses was where English uses how, in an exclamation. aufthun is separable, and that is the 1857 spelling of tat. He is twelve years old and has not seen daylight since he was two.

sentences.t: Er stand da und staunte alles an, als wenn er nicht recht gescheidt wäre.
sentences.l: He stood there and gazed at everything, as if he were not quite in his right mind.
sentences.i: He stood there gazing at everything, as if he were not quite in his right mind.
sentences.n: anstaunen is to gaze at in wonder, separable, with its an at the end. “als wenn” with the subjunctive is as if. gescheidt is the 1857 spelling of gescheit, clever, sane.

sentences.t: Die Mutter suchte den Weg nach Haus, und als sie ein paar Stunden gegangen waren, so kamen sie glücklich in ihr einsames Thal und zu ihrem Häuschen.
sentences.l: The mother sought the way home, and when they had walked a couple of hours, they came happily into their lonely valley and to their little house.
sentences.i: The mother looked for the way home, and when they had walked a couple of hours they came safely into their lonely valley and to their little house.
sentences.n: glücklich here is safely, successfully, rather than happily — the sense English keeps in they arrived safe. gehen forms its perfect with sein, “waren gegangen”, as verbs of motion do. Häuschen is a diminutive of Haus.

sentences.t: Der Vater saß unter der Thüre, er weinte vor Freude als er seine Frau erkannte und hörte daß Hans sein Sohn war, die er beide längst für todt gehalten hatte.
sentences.l: The father sat under the door, he wept for joy when he recognised his wife and heard that Hans was his son, whom he had both long since held for dead.
sentences.i: The father sat in the doorway; he wept for joy when he recognised his wife and heard that Hans was his son — the two of them he had long since given up for dead.
sentences.n: “unter der Thüre” is in the doorway, under the lintel. “vor Freude” gives the cause: from joy. “für todt halten” is to take for dead. The relative die reaches back over the whole sentence to gather both of them at once, which German manages and English cannot.

sentences.t: Aber Hans, obgleich erst zwölf Jahr alt, war doch einen Kopf größer als sein Vater.
sentences.l: But Hans, although only twelve years old, was yet a head taller than his father.
sentences.n: “einen Kopf größer” is a bare accusative of measure — taller by a head. obgleich is although, and its clause here has no verb of its own at all.

sentences.t: Sie giengen zusammen in das Stübchen, aber kaum hatte Hans seinen Sack auf die Ofenbank gesetzt, so fieng das ganze Haus an zu krachen, die Bank brach ein und dann auch der Fußboden, und der schwere Sack sank in den Keller hinab.
sentences.l: They went together into the little room, but scarcely had Hans set his sack on the stove-bench, then the whole house began to crack, the bench broke in and then the floor too, and the heavy sack sank down into the cellar.
sentences.i: They went together into the little room, but scarcely had Hans set his sack down on the stove bench when the whole house began to crack: the bench gave way, and then the floor too, and the heavy sack sank down into the cellar.
sentences.n: “kaum hatte er …, so …” puts the verb first after kaum and answers with so: scarcely had he, when. Die Ofenbank is the bench built against the stove, the warm seat of a peasant room. einbrechen and hinabsinken are both separable.

sentences.t: „Gott behüte uns,“ rief der Vater „was ist das? jetzt hast du unser Häuschen zerbrochen.“
sentences.l: “God preserve us,” cried the father, “what is that? now you have broken our little house to pieces.”
sentences.n: behüte is a subjunctive of wishing — may God keep us. The 1857 text prints no comma before “rief der Vater” and begins the next question with a small letter, both of them ordinary in this book.

sentences.t: „Laßt euch keine graue Haare darüber wachsen, lieber Vater,“ antwortete Hans, „da in dem Sack steckt mehr als für ein neues Haus nöthig ist.“
sentences.l: “Do not let yourselves any grey hairs grow over that, dear father,” answered Hans, “there in the sack there sits more than is necessary for a new house.”
sentences.i: “Do not let it grow you any grey hairs, dear father,” answered Hans, “there is more in that sack than a new house needs.”
sentences.n: Hans addresses his father with the plural Laßt and euch — the respectful old form a child used to a parent — where he used du to the robber captain. “sich keine grauen Haare wachsen lassen” is not to worry oneself grey over a thing. stecken is to be lodged, to sit inside.

sentences.t: Der Vater und Hans fiengen auch gleich an ein neues Haus zu bauen, Vieh zu erhandeln und Land zu kaufen und zu wirthschaften.
sentences.l: The father and Hans began at once to build a new house, to get cattle by bargaining and to buy land and to farm.
sentences.i: The father and Hans set to at once building a new house, buying up cattle, and purchasing land and farming it.
sentences.n: wirthschaften here is to farm, to manage land and stock — the 1857 spelling of wirtschaften. erhandeln is to acquire by trading. anfangen splits once and then governs four infinitives in a row.

sentences.t: Hans ackerte die Felder, und wenn er hinter dem Pflug gieng und ihn in die Erde hinein schob, so hatten die Stiere fast nicht nöthig zu ziehen.
sentences.l: Hans ploughed the fields, and when he walked behind the plough and pushed it into the earth in, the oxen had almost no need to pull.
sentences.i: Hans ploughed the fields, and when he walked behind the plough and drove it down into the earth, the oxen had hardly any need to pull.
sentences.n: “hinein schob” is printed as two words in 1857 where modern German writes hineinschob. “nöthig haben zu” is to have need to; nöthig is the 1857 spelling of nötig. Die Stiere are the draught oxen at the plough.

sentences.t: Den nächsten Frühling sagte Hans „Vater, behaltet alles Geld und laßt mir einen zentnerschweren Spazierstab machen, damit ich in die Fremde gehen kann.“
sentences.l: The next spring Hans said “father, keep all the money and have a hundredweight-heavy walking-staff made for me, so that I can go into the wide world.”
sentences.i: The next spring Hans said: “Father, keep all the money, and have a walking staff made for me weighing a hundredweight, so that I can go out into the world.”
sentences.n: behaltet and laßt are the plural imperatives again — he goes on speaking respectfully to his father. Ein Zentner is a hundredweight, about fifty kilos. “in die Fremde gehen” is to go out into foreign parts, away from home; die Fremde is a noun here, not an adjective. “Den nächsten Frühling” is a bare accusative of time.

sentences.t: Als der verlangte Stab fertig war, verließ er seines Vaters Haus, zog fort und kam in einen tiefen und finstern Wald.
sentences.l: When the demanded staff was ready, he left his father’s house, drew away and came into a deep and dark wood.
sentences.i: When the staff he had asked for was ready, he left his father’s house, set off, and came into a deep dark wood.
sentences.n: “seines Vaters Haus” puts the genitive in front of its noun, an older order that now survives mainly in names and in poetry. fortziehen is to move off, to set out. verlangte is a past participle used as an adjective: the demanded staff.

sentences.t: Da hörte er etwas knistern und knastern, schaute um sich und sah eine Tanne, die von unten bis oben wie ein Seil gewunden war:
sentences.l: Then he heard something crackle and crunch, looked about him and saw a fir tree that was twisted from below to above like a rope:
sentences.i: Then he heard something crackling and creaking, looked about him, and saw a fir tree twisted from bottom to top like a rope;
sentences.n: knistern und knastern is a made pair, the second word invented to answer the first — German builds such pairs freely, as in klipp und klapp. hören takes a bare infinitive: heard something crackle. gewunden is the past participle of winden, to wind, to twist.

sentences.t: und wie er die Augen in die Höhe richtete, so erblickte er einen großen Kerl, der den Baum gepackt hatte und ihn wie eine Weidenruthe umdrehte.
sentences.l: and as he directed his eyes up into the height, he caught sight of a great fellow who had seized the tree and was twisting it round like a willow switch.
sentences.i: and when he turned his eyes upward he caught sight of a great fellow who had taken hold of the tree and was twisting it about like a willow switch.
sentences.n: “die Augen in die Höhe richten” is to turn one’s eyes upward; richten is to direct, to aim. Eine Weidenruthe is a willow withy, the supple rod used for binding faggots — the comparison measures the man’s strength exactly.

sentences.t: „He!“ rief Hans, „was machst du da droben?“
sentences.l: “Hey!” cried Hans, “what are you doing up there?”
sentences.n: he is a shout to hail somebody — hey, hallo — and not the pronoun. droben is up there, aloft, contracted out of da oben.

sentences.t: Der Kerl antwortete „ich habe gestern Reiswellen zusammen getragen und will mir ein Seil dazu drehen.“
sentences.l: The fellow answered “I carried faggots together yesterday and want to twist myself a rope for them.”
sentences.i: The fellow answered: “I gathered faggots yesterday, and now I want to twist myself a rope to bind them with.”
sentences.n: Reiswellen are bundles of brushwood — Reis here is a twig, not rice. “zusammen getragen” is printed as two words. dazu is for that purpose, to go with them. He proposes to make his rope out of a whole fir tree, and says so as though it were the obvious thing.

sentences.t: „Das laß ich mir gefallen,“ dachte Hans, „der hat Kräfte,“ und rief ihm zu, „laß du das gut sein und komm mit mir.“
sentences.l: “That I let please me,” thought Hans, “he has strength,” and called across to him, “let that be good and come with me.”
sentences.i: “That is something I like,” thought Hans, “he has strength in him” — and he called across to him: “Leave that alone and come with me.”
sentences.n: “sich etwas gefallen lassen” is to let a thing suit one, to be content with it; here it is approval — that I call something. “laß … gut sein” is to let a matter rest, to leave it be. zurufen is separable and zu closes the clause. laß du puts the pronoun in after the imperative for weight: you there, leave it.

sentences.t: Der Kerl kletterte von oben herab, und war einen ganzen Kopf größer als Hans, und der war doch auch nicht klein.
sentences.l: The fellow climbed down from above, and was a whole head taller than Hans, and he was not small either.
sentences.i: The fellow climbed down from above, and was a whole head taller than Hans — and Hans was no small man.
sentences.n: “und der war doch auch nicht klein” uses der as a demonstrative pointing back at Hans: and he, mind you, was not small. herabklettern is separable.

sentences.t: „Du heißest jetzt Tannendreher“ sagte Hans zu ihm.
sentences.l: “You are called Fir-twister now,” said Hans to him.
sentences.i: “Your name is Fir-twister now,” said Hans to him.
sentences.n: Tannendreher is a transparent nickname — Tanne, fir, and drehen, to twist — and Hans simply confers it; the second companion will get his the same way. The 1857 text prints no comma before sagte.

sentences.t: Sie giengen darauf weiter und hörten etwas klopfen und hämmern, so stark daß bei jedem Schlag der Erdboden zitterte.
sentences.l: They went on after that and heard something knocking and hammering, so strong that at every blow the ground trembled.
sentences.i: They went on after that, and heard a knocking and hammering so loud that the ground trembled at every blow.
sentences.n: hören again takes bare infinitives — heard something knock and hammer. The tale announces its next companion by sound before it shows him, exactly as it did the first.

sentences.t: Bald darauf kamen sie zu einem mächtigen Felsen, vor dem stand ein Riese und schlug mit der Faust große Stücke davon ab.
sentences.l: Soon after that they came to a mighty rock, before which stood a giant and struck great pieces off it with his fist.
sentences.i: Soon after they came to a mighty rock, before which stood a giant striking great pieces off it with his fist.
sentences.n: “vor dem stand ein Riese” starts as a relative clause and goes on like a main one — German slides out of the relative into plain narrative without repairing the join, and this book does it often. abschlagen is separable, and its ab reaches the end after davon.

sentences.t: Als Hans fragte was er da vor hätte, antwortete er „wenn ich Nachts schlafen will, so kommen Bären, Wölfe und anderes Ungeziefer der Art, die schnuppern und schnuffeln an mir herum und lassen mich nicht schlafen, da will ich mir ein Haus bauen und mich hinein legen, damit ich Ruhe habe.“
sentences.l: When Hans asked what he had in mind there, he answered “when I want to sleep at night, then bears, wolves and other vermin of the kind come, they sniff and snuffle about me and do not let me sleep, so I want to build myself a house and lay myself inside, so that I have peace.”
sentences.i: When Hans asked what he had in mind, he answered: “When I want to sleep at night, bears and wolves and other vermin of the sort come and sniff and snuffle about me and will not let me sleep; so I mean to build myself a house and lie down inside it, and have some peace.”
sentences.n: vorhaben is to have in mind, to intend, and here it is split right across the clause: “was er da vor hätte”. Ungeziefer is vermin, and a giant’s reckoning of what counts as vermin runs to bears. schnuppern und schnuffeln is another made pair. hätte is the subjunctive of the reported question.

sentences.t: „Ei ja wohl,“ dachte Hans, „den kannst du auch noch brauchen“ und sprach zu ihm „laß das Hausbauen gut sein und geh mit mir, du sollst der Felsenklipperer heißen.“
sentences.l: “Ah, indeed,” thought Hans, “this one you can use as well” and spoke to him “let the house-building be good and go with me, you shall be called Rock-chipper.”
sentences.i: “Ah, indeed,” thought Hans, “here is another I can use” — and he said to him: “Leave the house-building be and come with me; your name shall be Rock-chipper.”
sentences.n: ei is a soft interjection, well now, ah. den is a demonstrative standing first for emphasis: this one. Hans thinks of himself as du, which German does easily. Felsenklipperer is Fels, rock, with klippern, to chip and knock — another transparent nickname; a few lines further on the tale will call the same man Steinklipperer, Stone-chipper, and never settle on one of the two.

sentences.t: Er willigte ein, und sie strichen alle drei durch den Wald hin und wo sie hinkamen, da wurden die wilden Thiere aufgeschreckt und liefen vor ihnen weg.
sentences.l: He consented, and all three ranged through the wood along, and wherever they came, there the wild beasts were startled up and ran away before them.
sentences.i: He consented, and the three of them ranged on through the wood, and wherever they came the wild beasts were startled up and ran away before them.
sentences.n: streichen said of men or animals is to range, to rove — not to stroke; “durch den Wald streichen” is to go ranging through the wood. einwilligen is separable. Thiere is the 1857 spelling of Tiere.

sentences.t: Abends kamen sie in ein altes verlassenes Schloß, stiegen hinauf und legten sich in den Saal schlafen.
sentences.l: In the evening they came into an old abandoned castle, climbed up and laid themselves down in the hall to sleep.
sentences.i: In the evening they came to an old abandoned castle, climbed up, and lay down to sleep in the hall.
sentences.n: Abends is an adverb built from a genitive: of an evening. “sich schlafen legen” is to lay oneself down to sleep, with the infinitive tacked on at the end. Nobody asks whose castle it is, and the tale never says.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen gieng Hans hinab in den Garten, der war ganz verwildert und stand voll Dörner und Gebüsch.
sentences.l: The next morning Hans went down into the garden, it was quite run wild and stood full of thorns and bushes.
sentences.i: The next morning Hans went down into the garden; it had run quite wild and stood full of thorns and scrub.
sentences.n: “der war ganz verwildert” is a demonstrative again, not a relative: the German begins a new statement about the garden. verwildern is to go wild, to run to waste. “stand voll” takes its complement with no article at all.

sentences.t: Und wie er so herum gieng, sprang ein Wildschwein auf ihn los: er gab ihm aber mit seinem Stab einen Schlag daß es gleich niederfiel.
sentences.l: And as he was walking about so, a wild boar sprang at him: but he gave it with his staff such a blow that it fell down at once.
sentences.i: And as he was walking about, a wild boar sprang at him; but he gave it such a blow with his staff that it fell down on the spot.
sentences.n: “losspringen auf” is to spring at, to launch oneself at; los as a particle carries the sense of breaking loose. “herum gieng” is printed as two words. daß with no preceding so still carries the force of so that.

sentences.t: Dann nahm er es auf die Schulter und brachte es hinauf; da steckten sie es an einen Spieß, machten sich einen Braten zurecht und waren guter Dinge.
sentences.l: Then he took it on his shoulder and carried it up; there they stuck it on a spit, made themselves a roast ready and were of good things.
sentences.i: Then he took it on his shoulder and carried it up; there they put it on a spit, got a roast ready, and were in good spirits.
sentences.n: “guter Dinge sein” is to be in good spirits, and takes a bare genitive plural with no preposition. zurechtmachen is to get a thing ready, and splits. Nothing is squeamish here: the boar is killed and eaten inside one sentence.

sentences.t: Nun verabredeten sie daß jeden Tag, der Reihe nach zwei auf die Jagd gehen sollten und einer daheim bleiben und kochen, für jeden neun Pfund Fleisch.
sentences.l: Now they arranged that every day, in turn, two should go to the hunt and one stay at home and cook, for each nine pounds of meat.
sentences.i: Now they arranged that every day, in turn, two should go hunting and one stay at home and cook — nine pounds of meat for each man.
sentences.n: “der Reihe nach” is in turn, one after another. The second sollten is left out and has to be carried over from the first: one should stay and cook. Nine pounds of meat a man is the measure of them, and the arithmetic matters as soon as the dwarf asks for a share.

sentences.t: Den ersten Tag blieb der Tannendreher daheim und Hans und der Felsenklipperer giengen auf die Jagd.
sentences.l: The first day Fir-twister stayed at home and Hans and Rock-chipper went to the hunt.
sentences.i: The first day Fir-twister stayed at home, and Hans and Rock-chipper went hunting.
sentences.n: “Den ersten Tag” is a bare accusative of time again. daheim is at home — the older southern word beside zu Hause, and this book uses it throughout.

sentences.t: Als der Tannendreher beim Kochen beschäftigt war, kam ein kleines altes zusammengeschrumpeltes Männchen zu ihm auf das Schloß, und forderte Fleisch.
sentences.l: When Fir-twister was busy at the cooking, a little old shrivelled-together mannikin came to him up at the castle, and demanded meat.
sentences.i: While Fir-twister was busy cooking, a little old shrivelled mannikin came up to him at the castle and demanded meat.
sentences.n: “beim Kochen” turns a verb into a noun after a preposition: at the cooking. zusammengeschrumpelt is a compound participle, shrivelled up together. This creature is called a Männchen and a Männlein here and a Zwerg, a dwarf, further on; the tale uses all three names for the same being and never explains what it is.

sentences.t: „Pack dich, Duckmäuser,“ antwortete er, „du brauchst kein Fleisch.“
sentences.l: “Take yourself off, sneak,” he answered, “you need no meat.”
sentences.i: “Be off with you, sneak,” he answered, “you have no need of meat.”
sentences.n: “sich packen” is to pack oneself off, to clear out — an imperative of pure contempt. Ein Duckmäuser is one who ducks and creeps, a sly cringing person. brauchen takes a bare accusative: to have need of a thing.

sentences.t: Aber wie verwunderte sich der Tannendreher, als das kleine unscheinbare Männlein an ihm hinauf sprang und mit Fäusten so auf ihn losschlug, daß er sich nicht wehren konnte, zur Erde fiel und nach Athem schnappte.
sentences.l: But how Fir-twister was astonished, when the little insignificant mannikin sprang up at him and struck at him so with its fists that he could not defend himself, fell to the earth and snapped for breath.
sentences.i: But how astonished Fir-twister was when the little insignificant mannikin sprang up at him and laid about him with its fists so that he could not defend himself, but fell to the ground and gasped for breath.
sentences.n: “wie verwunderte sich …” is an exclamation, not a question: how astonished he was. unscheinbar is unimpressive to look at, literally not shining out. “hinauf sprang” is printed as two words. Athem is the 1857 spelling of Atem.

sentences.t: Das Männlein gieng nicht eher fort, als bis es seinen Zorn völlig an ihm ausgelassen hatte.
sentences.l: The mannikin did not go away sooner than until it had let out its anger on him completely.
sentences.i: The mannikin did not go away until it had let out its whole rage on him.
sentences.n: “nicht eher … als bis” is a doubled construction: not before … until. “seinen Zorn an jemandem auslassen” is to vent one’s anger on somebody, and is still current German. fortgehen and auslassen both split.

sentences.t: Als die zwei andern von der Jagd heimkamen, sagte ihnen der Tannendreher nichts von dem alten Männchen und den Schlägen, die er bekommen hatte und dachte „wenn sie daheim bleiben, so können sies auch einmal mit der kleinen Kratzbürste versuchen,“
sentences.l: When the two others came home from the hunt, Fir-twister said nothing to them of the old mannikin and the blows that he had got, and thought “if they stay at home, then they can try it too for once with the little scratching-brush,”
sentences.i: When the two others came home from the hunt, Fir-twister said nothing to them of the old mannikin or of the blows he had taken, and thought: “If they stay at home, they can have a turn at the little scratching-brush themselves,”
sentences.n: Eine Kratzbürste is a scratching-brush, and as a name for a person one who scratches and bristles; the modern sense is a shrew. sies is sie es, they it. His silence is what sets the next two scenes going.

sentences.t: und der bloße Gedanke machte ihm schon Vergnügen.
sentences.l: and the bare thought already made him pleasure.
sentences.i: and the mere thought of it already gave him pleasure.
sentences.n: bloß here is mere, nothing but. “jemandem Vergnügen machen” is to give somebody pleasure, with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Den folgenden Tag blieb der Steinklipperer daheim, und dem gieng es gerade so wie dem Tannendreher, er ward von dem Männlein übel zugerichtet, weil er ihm kein Fleisch hatte geben wollen.
sentences.l: The following day Stone-chipper stayed at home, and it went with him just so as with Fir-twister, he was badly knocked about by the mannikin, because he had not wanted to give it any meat.
sentences.i: The next day Stone-chipper stayed at home, and it went with him exactly as it had with Fir-twister: he was badly knocked about by the mannikin, because he had refused to give it any meat.
sentences.n: The tale calls him Steinklipperer here, Stone-chipper, where it named him Felsenklipperer, Rock-chipper, a few lines back; the 1857 printing simply does not hold the name steady, and nothing is being tidied up here. “es geht jemandem so” is things go thus with a person, with the person in the dative. “hatte geben wollen” puts the modal into the infinitive at the end.

sentences.t: Als die andern Abends nach Haus kamen, sah es ihm der Tannendreher wohl an was er erfahren hatte, aber beide schwiegen still und dachten „der Hans muß auch von der Suppe kosten.“
sentences.l: When the others came home in the evening, Fir-twister saw it well off him what he had gone through, but both kept silent and thought “Hans must taste of the soup too.”
sentences.i: When the others came home in the evening, Fir-twister could see well enough by looking at him what he had been through; but both kept silent and thought: “Hans must have a taste of the soup as well.”
sentences.n: “einem etwas ansehen” is to tell a thing by looking at somebody, and ansehen splits, its an coming at the end. kosten here is to taste, not to cost — “von der Suppe kosten” is to get a taste of the same treatment. erfahren is to undergo, to find out by experience.

sentences.t: Der Hans, der den nächsten Tag daheim bleiben mußte, that seine Arbeit in der Küche, wie sichs gebührte, und als er oben stand und den Kessel abschaumte, kam das Männchen und forderte ohne weiteres ein Stück Fleisch.
sentences.l: Hans, who had to stay at home the next day, did his work in the kitchen as was fitting, and when he stood over it and skimmed the kettle, the mannikin came and demanded without more ado a piece of meat.
sentences.i: Hans, who had to stay at home the next day, did his work in the kitchen as was proper; and while he stood over the kettle skimming it, the mannikin came and demanded a piece of meat without more ado.
sentences.n: “wie sichs gebührte” is as was fitting, with sichs for sich es. abschaumen is to take the scum off a boiling pot; modern German writes abschäumen. “ohne weiteres” is without more ado, without further asking.

sentences.t: Da dachte Hans „es ist ein armer Wicht, ich will ihm von meinem Antheil geben, damit die andern nicht zu kurz kommen“ und reichte ihm ein Stück Fleisch.
sentences.l: Then Hans thought “it is a poor wight, I will give it of my share, so that the others do not come too short” and handed it a piece of meat.
sentences.i: Then Hans thought: “It is a poor wretch — I will give it some of my own share, so that the others are not short,” and he handed it a piece of meat.
sentences.n: Wicht is the same old word as the English wight: a creature, and in pity a poor little thing. Antheil is the 1857 spelling of Anteil, share. “zu kurz kommen” is to come off badly, to get less than one’s due. Hans’s answer to the demand is arithmetic — he pays out of his own nine pounds, and that, not softness, is what makes the difference.

sentences.t: Als es der Zwerg verzehrt hatte, verlangte er nochmals Fleisch, und der gutmüthige Hans gab es ihm und sagte da wäre noch ein schönes Stück, damit sollte er zufrieden sein.
sentences.l: When the dwarf had eaten it up, he demanded meat once more, and the good-natured Hans gave it to him and said there was a fine piece yet, with that he should be content.
sentences.i: When the dwarf had eaten it up he demanded meat once more, and good-natured Hans gave it him, and said there was still a fine piece, and with that he should be content.
sentences.n: The creature is now called der Zwerg, the dwarf, having been Männchen and Männlein a moment ago. wäre and sollte are the subjunctive of reported speech, which is how the German gives Hans’s words with no quotation marks. gutmüthig is the 1857 spelling of gutmütig.

sentences.t: Der Zwerg forderte aber zum drittenmal.
sentences.l: But the dwarf demanded a third time.
sentences.n: The third demand is the one that breaks the pattern — twice given and refused the third time, which is how these tales count. Everything that follows hangs on this one refusal.

sentences.t: „Du wirst unverschämt“ sagte Hans und gab ihm nichts.
sentences.l: “You are getting impudent,” said Hans and gave him nothing.
sentences.n: werden with an adjective is to become, to be getting: a state under way rather than a settled one. The 1857 text prints no comma before sagte.

sentences.t: Da wollte der boshafte Zwerg an ihm hinaufspringen und ihn wie den Tannendreher und Felsenklipperer behandeln, aber er kam an den unrechten.
sentences.l: Then the spiteful dwarf wanted to spring up at him and treat him like Fir-twister and Rock-chipper, but he came to the wrong one.
sentences.i: Then the spiteful dwarf made to spring up at him and treat him as it had treated Fir-twister and Rock-chipper — but it had come to the wrong man.
sentences.n: “an den unrechten kommen” is to come to the wrong man, to pick on the wrong person, and the phrase is still used. wollen here is not want but was about to. The dwarf is masculine, er, though the same being was a neuter Männlein a page ago.

sentences.t: Hans gab ihm, ohne sich anzustrengen, ein paar Hiebe, daß er die Schloßtreppe hinabsprang.
sentences.l: Hans gave him, without exerting himself, a couple of blows, so that he sprang down the castle stairs.
sentences.i: Hans gave it a couple of blows without even exerting himself, so that it went leaping down the castle stairs.
sentences.n: “ohne … anzustrengen” is the ohne + zu construction, with the zu slipped inside the separable verb: anzustrengen. hinabspringen is separable, and the stairs stand in the accusative as the way travelled.

sentences.t: Hans wollte ihm nachlaufen, fiel aber, so lang er war, über ihn hin.
sentences.l: Hans wanted to run after him, but fell, as long as he was, right over him.
sentences.i: Hans meant to run after it, but fell full length over it.
sentences.n: “so lang er war” is at his full length — the whole of him on the ground. nachlaufen takes the dative, ihm. “über ihn hin” keeps hin at the end for the direction of the fall.

sentences.t: Als er sich wieder aufgerichtet hatte, war ihm der Zwerg voraus.
sentences.l: When he had raised himself up again, the dwarf was ahead of him.
sentences.i: By the time he had picked himself up again, the dwarf had got ahead of him.
sentences.n: “sich aufrichten” is to straighten up, and separates. voraus with the dative is ahead of, in front of.

sentences.t: Hans eilte ihm bis in den Wald nach und sah wie er in eine Felsenhöhle schlüpfte.
sentences.l: Hans hurried after him as far as into the wood and saw how he slipped into a rock-cave.
sentences.i: Hans hurried after it as far as the wood, and saw it slip into a cave in the rocks.
sentences.n: nacheilen is separable and its nach travels all the way to the end, past the whole phrase of direction. wie after a verb of seeing needs no English word of its own.

sentences.t: Hans kehrte nun heim, hatte sich aber die Stelle gemerkt.
sentences.l: Hans now turned home, but had marked the place for himself.
sentences.i: Hans now turned homeward, but he had marked the place well.
sentences.n: “sich etwas merken” is to fix a thing in one’s memory, with the dative sich of advantage. heimkehren splits.

sentences.t: Die beiden andern, als sie nach Haus kamen, wunderten sich daß Hans so wohl auf war.
sentences.l: The two others, when they came home, wondered that Hans was so well up.
sentences.i: The other two, when they came home, wondered to find Hans so hale and hearty.
sentences.n: “wohl auf”, printed as two words here, is the modern wohlauf: in good trim, none the worse. “sich wundern daß” is to be surprised that. What surprises them is exactly what they had arranged not to warn him about.

sentences.t: Er erzählte ihnen was sich zugetragen hatte, und da verschwiegen sie nicht länger wie es ihnen ergangen war.
sentences.l: He told them what had come to pass, and then they no longer kept silent about how it had gone with them.
sentences.i: He told them what had happened, and then they no longer kept silent about how it had gone with them.
sentences.n: “sich zutragen” is to come to pass, and separates. verschweigen is to keep a thing back, to hold it in silence — the ver- turns schweigen from being silent into silencing a matter. “es ist mir ergangen” is things went thus with me.

sentences.t: Hans lachte und sagte „es ist euch ganz recht, warum seid ihr so geitzig mit eurem Fleisch gewesen, aber es ist eine Schande, ihr seid so groß und habt euch von dem Zwerge Schläge geben lassen.“
sentences.l: Hans laughed and said “it is quite right for you, why were you so stingy with your meat, but it is a disgrace, you are so big and have let yourselves be given blows by the dwarf.”
sentences.i: Hans laughed and said: “It serves you quite right — why were you so stingy with your meat? But it is a disgrace: you are such big fellows, and you let the dwarf beat you.”
sentences.n: “es ist dir recht” is it serves you right. geitzig is the 1857 spelling of geizig, stingy. “sich Schläge geben lassen” is the roundabout German passive built with lassen: to let blows be given oneself. dem Zwerge keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Sie nahmen darauf Korb und Seil und giengen alle drei zu der Felsenhöhle, in welche der Zwerg geschlüpft war, und ließen den Hans mit seinem Stab im Korb hinab.
sentences.l: They took basket and rope after that and all three went to the rock-cave into which the dwarf had slipped, and let Hans down with his staff in the basket.
sentences.i: After that they took basket and rope, and all three went to the cave in the rocks into which the dwarf had slipped, and let Hans down in the basket with his staff.
sentences.n: Korb und Seil stand without articles, as a named pair of tools often does. hinablassen splits and hinab closes the clause. The cave in the rock has quietly become a shaft you are lowered into, and the tale does not stop to reconcile the two.

sentences.t: Als Hans auf dem Grund angelangt war, fand er eine Thüre, und als er sie öffnete, saß da eine bildschöne Jungfrau, nein so schön, daß es nicht zu sagen ist, und neben ihr saß der Zwerg und grinste den Hans an wie eine Meerkatze.
sentences.l: When Hans had arrived at the bottom, he found a door, and when he opened it, there sat a picture-beautiful maiden, no, so beautiful that it is not to be said, and beside her sat the dwarf and grinned at Hans like a long-tailed monkey.
sentences.i: When Hans had reached the bottom he found a door, and when he opened it there sat a maiden as beautiful as a picture — no, so beautiful that it cannot be told — and beside her sat the dwarf, grinning at Hans like a monkey.
sentences.n: bildschön is picture-beautiful. The teller breaks off in the middle of his own sentence with nein to say that the description will not do; the printing keeps that spoken gesture. “es ist nicht zu sagen” is the sein + zu construction: it is not to be said, it cannot be told. Eine Meerkatze is a long-tailed monkey, the kind shown at fairs. angrinsen splits: “grinste … an”.

sentences.t: Sie aber war mit Ketten gebunden und blickte ihn so traurig an, daß Hans großes Mitleid empfand und dachte „du mußt sie aus der Gewalt des bösen Zwerges erlösen,“ und gab ihm einen Streich mit seinem Stab, daß er todt niedersank.
sentences.l: But she was bound with chains and looked at him so sadly that Hans felt great pity and thought “you must deliver her out of the power of the wicked dwarf,” and gave him a stroke with his staff, so that he sank down dead.
sentences.i: But she was bound with chains, and looked at him so sadly that Hans felt great pity and thought: “You must deliver her out of the wicked dwarf’s power” — and he gave the dwarf such a stroke with his staff that he sank down dead.
sentences.n: ein Streich here is a blow, a stroke of the staff; the same word later comes to mean a trick or a prank. Hans addresses himself as du in his own thoughts, which German does without any awkwardness. anblicken splits. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot. The pity and the killing arrive in the same sentence, and the tale does not weigh one against the other.

sentences.t: Alsbald fielen die Ketten von der Jungfrau ab, und Hans war wie verzückt über ihre Schönheit.
sentences.l: At once the chains fell off from the maiden, and Hans was as if enraptured over her beauty.
sentences.i: At once the chains fell away from the maiden, and Hans was as one enraptured by her beauty.
sentences.n: abfallen splits, and ab arrives at the end. alsbald is at once, presently — an elevated old word this book is fond of. verzückt is carried out of oneself, entranced.

sentences.t: Sie erzählte ihm sie wäre eine Königstochter, die ein wilder Graf aus ihrer Heimath geraubt und hier in den Felsen eingesperrt hätte, weil sie nichts von ihm hätte wissen wollen:
sentences.l: She told him she was a king’s-daughter whom a wild count had carried off out of her homeland and shut up here in the rocks, because she had not wanted to know anything of him:
sentences.i: She told him that she was a king’s daughter, whom a wild count had carried off from her homeland and shut up here in the rocks, because she would have nothing to do with him;
sentences.n: Everything she says stands in the subjunctive — wäre, hätte, hätte wissen wollen — because it is reported, and German can hold that key for a whole sentence without one she said. “nichts von jemandem wissen wollen” is to want nothing to do with somebody. Heimath is the 1857 spelling of Heimat.

sentences.t: den Zwerg aber hätte der Graf zum Wächter gesetzt und er hätte ihr Leid und Drangsal genug angethan.
sentences.l: but the dwarf the count had set as a watchman and he had done her sorrow and affliction enough.
sentences.i: but the count had set the dwarf there as her guard, and he had done her sorrow and affliction enough.
sentences.n: The object den Zwerg comes first for emphasis, so the verb follows it and the subject der Graf comes third. “zum Wächter setzen” is to set somebody as a watchman. Drangsal is affliction, hardship — an old and rather biblical word. angethan is the 1857 spelling of angetan.

sentences.t: Darauf setzte Hans die Jungfrau in den Korb und ließ sie hinauf ziehen.
sentences.l: Thereupon Hans set the maiden into the basket and let her be drawn up.
sentences.i: Thereupon Hans set the maiden in the basket and had her drawn up.
sentences.n: lassen once again does the work English does with have: had her pulled up. “hinauf ziehen” is printed as two words.

sentences.t: Der Korb kam wieder herab, aber Hans traute den beiden Gesellen nicht und dachte „sie haben sich schon falsch gezeigt und dir nichts von dem Zwerg gesagt, wer weiß was sie gegen dich im Schild führen.“
sentences.l: The basket came down again, but Hans did not trust the two companions and thought “they have already shown themselves false and told you nothing of the dwarf, who knows what they are carrying against you in their shield.”
sentences.i: The basket came down again, but Hans did not trust the two companions, and thought: “They have shown themselves false already and told you nothing about the dwarf; who knows what they are plotting against you.”
sentences.n: “etwas im Schilde führen” is to be up to something, to have a design: der Schild is the knight’s shield, and the device he carried on it declared who he was and what he was about. weiß here is the verb wissen, to know, and not the adjective weiß, white — the two are spelled alike. trauen takes the dative.

sentences.t: Da legte er seinen Stab in den Korb, und das war sein Glück, denn als der Korb halb in der Höhe war, ließen sie ihn fallen, und hätte Hans wirklich darin gesessen, so wäre es sein Tod gewesen.
sentences.l: Then he laid his staff into the basket, and that was his good fortune, for when the basket was half up in the height, they let it fall, and had Hans really been sitting in it, then it would have been his death.
sentences.i: So he laid his staff in the basket, and that was his good fortune, for when the basket was half way up they let it fall; and if Hans had really been sitting in it, it would have been his death.
sentences.n: “hätte Hans wirklich darin gesessen” is a conditional with no wenn: German puts the verb first and means if. “fallen lassen” is to let fall, with the bare infinitive.

sentences.t: Aber nun wußte er nicht wie er sich aus der Tiefe herausarbeiten sollte und wie er hin und her dachte, er fand keinen Rath.
sentences.l: But now he did not know how he should work himself out of the deep, and however he thought this way and that, he found no counsel.
sentences.i: But now he did not know how he was to work his way out of the deep, and however he turned it over in his mind, he found no way out.
sentences.n: die Tiefe is the noun formed from tief: the deep, the depths. “hin und her denken” is to think a thing this way and that. “keinen Rath finden” is to find no remedy, no way out; Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat, counsel.

sentences.t: „Es ist doch traurig,“ sagte er „daß du da unten verschmachten sollst.“
sentences.l: “It is sad indeed,” he said, “that you are to languish down there.”
sentences.i: “It is a sad thing,” he said, “that you should languish away down here.”
sentences.n: He addresses himself as du and speaks of himself as though he stood somewhere else — “da unten”, down there. verschmachten is to pine away, to perish of hunger or thirst. This is the tale’s one moment of self-pity, and it lasts a single sentence.

sentences.t: Und als er so auf und abgieng, kam er wieder zu dem Kämmerchen, wo die Jungfrau gesessen hatte, und sah daß der Zwerg einen Ring am Finger hatte, der glänzte und schimmerte.
sentences.l: And as he walked so up and down, he came again to the little chamber where the maiden had sat, and saw that the dwarf had a ring on his finger which gleamed and shimmered.
sentences.n: “auf und ab gehen” is to walk to and fro, and abgieng here is the second half of that pair rather than a verb of its own. Kämmerchen is a diminutive of Kammer. The ring has been on the dwarf’s hand since Hans first saw him, and the tale mentions it only now that it is needed.

sentences.t: Da zog er ihn ab und steckte ihn an, und als er ihn am Finger umdrehte, so hörte er plötzlich etwas über seinem Kopf rauschen.
sentences.l: Then he drew it off and put it on, and when he turned it round on his finger, he suddenly heard something rushing above his head.
sentences.n: abziehen and anstecken are both separable and both leave their particles at the end — off and on, in two short clauses. rauschen is a verb here, after hören: to rush, to rustle. Nothing has told Hans the ring is anything more than pretty; he turns it by accident.

sentences.t: Er blickte in die Höhe und sah da Luftgeister schweben, die sagten er wäre ihr Herr und fragten was sein Begehren wäre.
sentences.l: He looked up into the height and saw air-spirits hovering there, who said he was their lord and asked what his desire was.
sentences.i: He looked up and saw spirits of the air hovering there, who said that he was their lord and asked what his desire was.
sentences.n: Luftgeister are spirits of the air, and the compound says all the tale ever says about them. wäre twice marks reported speech. das Begehren is a noun made from the verb begehren, to desire. Where the ring came from, and why they obey it, is simply not told.

sentences.t: Hans war anfangs ganz verstummt, dann aber sagte er sie sollten ihn hinauf tragen.
sentences.l: Hans was at first quite struck dumb, but then he said they should carry him up.
sentences.i: Hans was struck quite dumb at first, but then he said they were to carry him up.
sentences.n: verstummen is to fall silent, to be struck dumb — the ver- makes stumm, dumb, into something that happens to a person. sollten is the subjunctive of the reported order. “hinauf tragen” is printed as two words.

sentences.t: Augenblicklich gehorchten sie, und es war nicht anders als flöge er hinauf.
sentences.l: Instantly they obeyed, and it was not otherwise than as if he flew up.
sentences.i: They obeyed instantly, and it was just as if he were flying upward.
sentences.n: “es war nicht anders als flöge er” is an as-if clause with no als ob: German drops the ob and puts the verb first. flöge is the past subjunctive of fliegen. gehorchen takes the dative.

sentences.t: Als er aber oben war, so war kein Mensch mehr zu sehen, und als er in das Schloß gieng, so fand er auch dort niemand.
sentences.l: But when he was up above, no person was any longer to be seen, and when he went into the castle, he found nobody there either.
sentences.i: But when he was up above, there was not a soul to be seen; and when he went into the castle, he found nobody there either.
sentences.n: “zu sehen sein” is the sein + zu construction again: to be seen, that is, visible. kein Mensch is the everyday German for nobody at all. so at the head of the main clause is a resumptive marker and needs no English word.

sentences.t: Der Tannendreher und der Felsenklipperer waren fortgeeilt und hatten die schöne Jungfrau mit geführt.
sentences.l: Fir-twister and Rock-chipper had hurried away and had carried the beautiful maiden along with them.
sentences.i: Fir-twister and Rock-chipper had hurried away and carried the beautiful maiden off with them.
sentences.n: “mit geführt” is printed as two words where modern German writes mitgeführt. forteilen forms its perfect with sein, as verbs of motion do. What the two of them meant to do with her the tale never says, and never comes back to.

sentences.t: Aber Hans drehte den Ring, da kamen die Luftgeister und sagten ihm die zwei wären auf dem Meer.
sentences.l: But Hans turned the ring, then the air-spirits came and told him the two were on the sea.
sentences.i: But Hans turned the ring, and the spirits of the air came and told him the two were on the sea.
sentences.n: wären is the subjunctive of what he was told. The ring has become the tale’s engine, and from here it does everything the cudgel and the staff did in the first half. How the companions reached the sea at all is left unexplained.

sentences.t: Hans lief und lief in einem fort bis er zu dem Meeresstrand kam, da erblickte er weit weit auf dem Wasser ein Schiffchen, in welchem seine treulosen Gefährten saßen.
sentences.l: Hans ran and ran on and on until he came to the sea-shore, there he caught sight far far out on the water of a little ship in which his faithless companions sat.
sentences.i: Hans ran and ran without stopping until he came to the sea-shore; there he caught sight, far far out on the water, of a little ship in which his faithless companions sat.
sentences.n: “in einem fort” is without a break, on and on. The repetitions — lief und lief, weit weit — are the teller’s own and are not a translator’s flourish. treulos is faithless, without troth.

sentences.t: Und im heftigen Zorn sprang er, ohne sich zu besinnen, mit sammt seinem Stab ins Wasser und fieng an zu schwimmen, aber der zentnerschwere Stab zog ihn tief hinab, daß er fast ertrunken wäre.
sentences.l: And in fierce rage he sprang, without stopping to think, together with his staff into the water and began to swim, but the hundredweight staff drew him deep down, so that he would almost have drowned.
sentences.i: And in fierce rage he sprang into the water without a moment’s thought, staff and all, and began to swim; but the hundredweight staff dragged him down deep, so that he was within an ace of drowning.
sentences.n: “sich besinnen” is to stop and think, to reflect, so “ohne sich zu besinnen” is without a moment’s thought. “mit sammt” is together with; sammt is the 1857 spelling of samt. The staff he had his fortune made from very nearly kills him.

sentences.t: Da drehte er noch zu rechter Zeit den Ring, alsbald kamen die Luftgeister und trugen ihn, so schnell wie der Blitz, in das Schiffchen.
sentences.l: Then he turned the ring just in time, at once the air-spirits came and carried him, as quick as lightning, into the little ship.
sentences.i: Then he turned the ring just in time; at once the spirits of the air came and carried him, quick as lightning, into the little ship.
sentences.n: “zu rechter Zeit” is in good time, at the right moment, and takes no article. “so schnell wie der Blitz” keeps the definite article where English drops it: quick as lightning.

sentences.t: Da schwang er seinen Stab und gab den bösen Gesellen den verdienten Lohn und warf sie hinab ins Wasser;
sentences.l: Then he swung his staff and gave the wicked companions the deserved reward and threw them down into the water;
sentences.i: Then he swung his staff, gave the wicked companions the reward they had earned, and threw them down into the water;
sentences.n: “den verdienten Lohn geben” is to pay a man the wages he has earned — said with a straight face of a beating and a drowning. hinabwerfen splits. The tale does not pause over it, and neither should the English.

sentences.t: dann aber ruderte er mit der schönen Jungfrau, die in den größten Ängsten gewesen war, und die er zum zweiten Male befreit hatte, heim zu ihrem Vater und ihrer Mutter, und ward mit ihr verheirathet, und haben alle sich gewaltig gefreut.
sentences.l: but then he rowed with the beautiful maiden, who had been in the greatest fears, and whom he had freed for the second time, home to her father and her mother, and was married to her, and all have rejoiced mightily.
sentences.i: but then he rowed the beautiful maiden — who had been in the greatest terror, and whom he had now freed a second time — home to her father and mother, and was married to her, and they all rejoiced mightily.
sentences.n: The sentence ends in the perfect, “haben alle sich gewaltig gefreut”, after a whole tale of the simple past: the teller steps out of the story to close it, as a story told aloud does. verheirathet is the 1857 spelling of verheiratet. Ängsten is a plural of Angst, terrors. The printing leaves its ends loose and does not tie them — nothing is said of how the two got from the castle to a ship at sea, and Hans’s own father and mother are never mentioned again.

glossary.angethan: anthun — done (to someone) (past part.; 1857 spelling of angetan; jemandem Leid anthun: to do a person harm)
glossary.besinnen: sich besinnen — to stop and think, to reflect (infinitive; ohne sich zu besinnen: without a moment’s thought)
glossary.blitz: der Blitz — lightning (so schnell wie der Blitz: quick as lightning)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun, and the impersonal subject of es war, es gieng)
glossary.fremde: die Fremde — foreign parts, the world away from home (in die Fremde gehen: to go out into the world)
glossary.gefallen: gefallen — to please (sich etwas gefallen lassen: to let a thing suit one, to approve of it)
glossary.gefährten: der Gefährte — companions (nom. pl.; seine treulosen Gefährten: his faithless companions)
glossary.gesetzt: setzen — set, put (past part.; auf die Bank setzen: to set on the bench; zum Wächter setzen: to set as a guard)
glossary.grund: der Grund — the bottom, the floor (auf dem Grund: at the bottom of the shaft)
glossary.he: he! — hey!, hallo! (a shout to hail someone; not the pronoun)
glossary.heißen: heißen — to be called, to be named (infinitive; du sollst … heißen: your name shall be — not the adjective heiß, hot)
glossary.hängen: hängen — to hang, to let hang (die Köpfe hängen: to let one’s head droop, of drowsy or dejected people)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, to it (dative of er and of es)
glossary.kehrte: heimkehren — turned homeward, went home (3rd sg. pret.; separable heim-)
glossary.ketten: die Kette — chains (dat. pl.; mit Ketten gebunden: bound with chains)
glossary.knüttel: der Knüttel — cudgel, heavy stick (acc. sg.; modern Knüppel)
glossary.kosten: kosten — to taste, to have a taste of (von der Suppe kosten: to taste the soup)
glossary.ließen: lassen — let (3rd pl. pret.; hinab lassen: to let down; fallen lassen: to let fall)
glossary.los: los — loose, off (here the particle of losspringen, to spring at: sprang auf ihn los)
glossary.rauschen: rauschen — to rush, to rustle (infinitive, here after hören: heard something rushing)
glossary.reihe: die Reihe — row, line; der Reihe nach — in turn, one after another
glossary.richtete: richten — directed, turned (3rd sg. pret.; die Augen in die Höhe richten: to turn one’s eyes upward)
glossary.sage: sagen — say!, tell! (imperative sg.; sage mir: tell me — not die Sage, a legend)
glossary.schild: der Schild — shield; etwas im Schilde führen — to be plotting something, to have a design
glossary.schwang: schwingen — swung (3rd sg. pret.; einen Stab schwingen: to swing a staff)
glossary.setzte: setzen — set, put (3rd sg. pret.; setzte sie in den Korb: set her in the basket)
glossary.streich: der Streich — a stroke, a blow (einen Streich geben: to deal a blow)
glossary.strichen: streichen — roamed, ranged, roved (3rd pl. pret.; durch den Wald streichen: to range through the wood)
glossary.tiefe: die Tiefe — the deep, the depths (fem. noun formed from tief)
glossary.wackerer: wacker — stout, sound, serviceable (masc. nom. sg.; said of a thing that will not fail you)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (he) knows (3rd sg. pres.; the same spelling is also weiß, white)
glossary.wirthschaften: wirthschaften — to farm, to keep house and manage the land (infinitive; 1857 spelling of wirtschaften)
glossary.wächter: der Wächter — watchman, guard (acc. sg.; zum Wächter setzen: to set someone as a guard)
glossary.zwerge: der Zwerg — dwarf (dat. sg. with the old -e; von dem Zwerge: by the dwarf)
